title: The Luxury Belief of the New Educational Establishment
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: This article delivers a sharp internal critique of the 'new educational establishment' — the movement broadly associated with E.D. Hirsch, knowledge-rich curricula, and cultural literacy — arguing that despite its evidence-based posture on instructional methods, it has uncritically adopted a very lightly-evidenced position on the purpose of schools. Stephen Vainker contrasts this with the older and more sensible conservative position articulated by Franklin Bobbitt and William Bagley: that schools should prepare children for adult life across three overlapping functions (socialisation, qualification, and personal development). The Hirsch tradition, the article argues, has reduced this rich vision to a singular obsession with building a shared stock of general knowledge — a hobby horse from an English professor that has become national education policy in England under Gove and Gibb without rigorous examination. The article shows that even early 20th-century conservative curriculum theorists explicitly endorsed a balance of knowledge and skills and warned against education becoming merely reproductive. Vainker's deeper critique is that the new educational establishment has swallowed Hirsch whole in reaction against progressive education, without recognising that the old conservatives they invoke never agreed with the narrow position they now take.
points: The new educational establishment is internally inconsistent: it rightly calls out myths (learning styles, zones of regulation) on evidence grounds, but simultaneously adopts Hirsch's cultural literacy argument — a polemic from an English lecturer with thin evidence — as unquestionable educational purpose.

The genuine conservative position on education, articulated by Bobbitt and Bagley in the early 20th century, held that schools should prepare students for adult life across three dimensions: socialisation, qualification, and personal development — a far richer vision than Hirsch's singular focus on shared cultural knowledge.

Even Bobbitt, whom the new establishment might cite in their favor, explicitly argued that schools must develop 'thought and judgment in connection with actual life-situations' and 'train every citizen for proficiency,' not merely for the reproduction of facts.

Hirsch's argument was built on a narrow claim about the role of background knowledge in reading comprehension, expanded into a sweeping claim about cultural literacy and national economic competitiveness — a move that Vainker argues was tenuous and strange.

Gove and Gibb converted Hirsch's polemic into English national education policy without judiciously considering its scope or consequences, in the process abandoning the richer conservative tradition of Bagley and Bobbitt that would have insisted education serve the whole child's preparation for life.
quotes: The new educational establishment pride themselves as evidence-based, often denouncing myths (learning styles, zones of regulation, etc.). But when it comes to the most important aspect of education — determining the very purpose of schools — they prove to be remarkably soft-headed.

Without due consideration, they have turned their backs on the established conservative position on the purpose of schools: that schools are to prepare children for adult life. Instead, they have swallowed whole the eccentric and very lightly-evidenced position of an English professor: that the purpose of schools is to ensure a common stock of general knowledge.

Education is now to develop a type of wisdom that can grow only out of participation in the living experiences of men, and never out of mere memorization of verbal statements of facts. It must, therefore, train thought and judgment in connection with actual life-situations, a task distinctly different from the cloistral activities of the past.

E.D. Hirsch was a particularly eccentric member of the reform movement who used the bandwagon of the crisis of improving the human capital produced by American schools to advance his particular hobby horse — that the amount of shared knowledge among Americans was declining. An English lecturer, he developed the notion that a society could not be meaningfully literate if it lacked a stock of general knowledge that could be assumed of all citizens.

In their ignorance and naivety, Gove and Gibb took one English lecturer's polemic about his hobby horse and turned it into national education policy. Rather than judiciously considering the huge impact that educational policy has on the lives of all children, they went all in on Hirsch, which had had the added pleasure of sticking it to the 'blob.'

He is not so much standing up for education to have a substantive purpose but merely over-emphasising a particular aspect of the purpose of education at the expense of a broader understanding of socialisation, bildung, and preparation for work. He is more footnote than iconoclast.
